objectives: Secure a negotiated settlement with the UK that lets the EU conclude the Article XXVIII process by June without derailing Council sign-off.
Preserve a workable, defensible TRQ design (country-specific share or equivalent mechanism for the UK) that reduces the risk of UK retaliation or a drawn-out compensation dispute.
Avoid pushing the UK into a joint front with Japan/Korea on FTA disapplication; keep the UK's dispute separate and bilateral.
Protect the EU's institutional credibility as a good-faith GATT Article XXVIII actor, since I face the same counterparts on future goods files.

Manage the FTA/TCA disapplication issue carefully — find language or carve-outs that limit UK grievance without abandoning the core policy objective of closing the non-market-economy circumvention route.
Where possible, link this to the UK's own steel safeguard/Article XXVIII process to find mutually acceptable trade-offs (e.g. EU quota treatment under UK measure) rather than pure compensation.
Keep Brussels informed with an accurate read of UK red lines and flexibility, so any mandate adjustment can be sought in time.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement (or clear path to one) that the UK capital can accept within the four rounds, preserving most of the EU's core measure (bound rate, global TRQ backbone, timeline) while giving the UK enough — a country-specific share, transitional arrangements, or reciprocal treatment under its own measure — that it does not retaliate or ally with Japan/Korea. Failure: no deal, UK withdraws equivalent concessions, and/or UK joins Japan/Korea in a joint retaliation/dispute strategy, damaging the EU's broader Geneva relationships and creating a tit-for-tat spiral with the UK's own steel measure just as it's being finalised.
declaration.approach: Open by restating the EU's rationale (non-market-economy overcapacity) to frame this as defensive, not UK-targeted, and signal genuine willingness to discuss allocation method and volume rather than just the headline numbers — since Brussels has given me flexibility on design, not just a fixed offer. Listen carefully in Phase 1 for what the UK actually prioritises (volume vs. FTA disapplication vs. duration/review clause) and use Phase 2 to test Brussels on realistic compensation instruments: a UK-specific quota share, phased-in FTA disapplication, or a review clause tied to a duration shorter than permanent. Try early to decouple the UK from Japan/Korea by treating the UK's substantial/principal-supplier status seriously and visibly, and by exploring linkage with the UK's own safeguard measure and EU quota treatment there, so the two processes can be traded against each other rather than escalate together. Avoid appearing to stonewall on the FTA disapplication point, since that's what's driving Japan/Korea's outreach — even symbolic movement there (timing, review clause, exemption threshold) could defuse the coalition risk. Keep tone cooperative and long-game oriented, since I'll be working with this UK counterpart on other files regardless of outcome here.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A country-specific or ring-fenced UK share of the TRQ well above a pure first-come-first-served global pool outcome, preservation or phased treatment of FTA/TCA preferences, a review clause and finite duration, and reciprocal favourable treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard. They will want to protect a concentrated, politically sensitive domestic industry and will be wary of setting a precedent that undermines their own TCA position. They may also want the credible option of retaliation or Japan/Korea alignment as leverage.

Timely conclusion by June to keep the Council vote on schedule, protection of the core policy objective (closing NME circumvention, permanent legal footing), minimal erosion of the headline TRQ/rate structure, and avoidance of a broader WTO dispute or coordinated retaliation that could complicate other files. Member states with steel production will push for a tight measure; steel-consuming member states will push for a workable UK deal to avoid input cost/political fallout.

To preserve their own larger volume shares and FTA preferences, and opportunistically to recruit the UK into a joint dispute over FTA disapplication to increase collective pressure on the EU. Their interest is in maximising leverage over the EU's overall TRQ design, not specifically in UK outcomes.

Similar to Japan/Korea — protection of their own volumes and principal-supplier claims, handled in separate tracks, but with an interest in whatever precedent the UK settlement sets for allocation methodology.

objectives: Secure UK agreement to the modification within the four rounds so Council can vote in June, while preserving the core architecture of the regime (permanent legal footing, meaningful tariff wall against non-market-economy overcapacity).
Keep the TRQ volume and out-of-quota rate close to the original proposal (400,000t global / 50%), conceding only what is necessary to secure agreement rather than what is merely requested.
If a country-specific or FTA-pool allocation is used, keep any UK-specific share modest and avoid setting a precedent that Turkey or Korea can then demand matching or larger treatment.
Protect the disapplication of FTA tariff reductions on UK-origin steel as a bargaining chip — trade it for something valuable rather than dropping it for free.
Obtain something concrete on EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own steel safeguard as reciprocal compensation, so this isn't a one-way concession from the EU side.
Avoid a precedent-setting review clause or sunset that would let the UK (or others) relitigate the regime every year; if a review clause is unavoidable, make it narrow and infrequent.

Manage member state politics: keep steel-producing member states satisfied that import volumes are genuinely constrained, while not alarming steel-consuming member states with excessive price/supply effects.

Avoid triggering a UK withdrawal of concessions that would hit EU exporters to the UK (3.6mt, 64% of UK steel imports) — a UK retaliation could be more costly to specific EU producers than the value of what we'd concede now.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a signed agreement by Round 4 that keeps the TRQ volume near 400,000t (or modestly above with clear conditions), preserves a meaningful out-of-quota rate (not eroded far below 50%), avoids an open-ended or generous FTA carve-out, and secures some reciprocal movement from the UK on its own safeguard treatment of EU exporters — concluded in time for the June Council vote. Failure: no deal (Council vote slips, UK retaliates within six months against EU exporters, and the file becomes hostage to the Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims setting adverse precedents), or a deal that guts the regime's protective effect (TRQ volume ballooned, rate cut sharply, UK carved out from FTA disapplication) such that steel-producing member states and the industry judge the regime toothless.
declaration.approach: Open firm on the original notified terms to anchor the negotiation and test UK priorities, since capitals cannot see each other and the UK's political exposure (concentrated production sites, employment) creates real pressure on their side to settle. Use the threat of the June deadline and no-deal default (which analysts say hurts the UK more) as leverage, but treat it as a genuine fallback I'm prepared to use if the UK's asks are structurally incompatible with a durable regime — I don't want to trade away the core architecture just to get a signature. Look for a package trade: modest TRQ increase or a UK-specific/product-specific carve-out on the narrower product range where UK exports concentrate, in exchange for UK movement on EU exporters' quota treatment under its own safeguard and acceptance of the FTA-disapplication principle. Keep any concession framed as compensation for equivalent value elsewhere in the schedule, not as a weakening of the steel regime itself, to protect the position with the Trade Policy Committee and Council. Hold back reserve concessions (e.g., a review clause, product carve-outs) for later rounds rather than opening with them, so I have room to move without collapsing the anchor.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum preserved tariff-free access for UK steel exporters (higher TRQ volume, UK-specific country share rather than pure global first-come-first-served, low or zero out-of-quota rate on lines where UK is concentrated), exemption from the FTA-disapplication clause via the TCA relationship, a review clause, and reciprocal favourable treatment for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard as part of any deal. They are under strong pressure to avoid a settlement that devastates concentrated production sites, but also want to protect their own parallel Article XXVIII/safeguard leverage over EU exporters.

Not directly at this table, but will want any UK settlement not to set a precedent of generous country-specific shares or carve-outs that they can then claim for themselves, given Turkey and Korea ship larger volumes than the UK. This constrains how generous I can be with the UK without inviting escalation elsewhere.

A tight, durable regime with minimal leakage — low TRQ volume, high out-of-quota rate, no generous FTA pool, quick conclusion so the measure is on a permanent footing before further NME-driven import surges.

Sufficient tariff-free volume and reasonable administration (avoiding pure first-come-first-served scarcity/price spikes) to protect input costs and supply chains; may push back if the regime is too restrictive.

Threatening retaliation over the EU's Article XXVIII actions generally, which raises the cost of dragging this process out or of the EU being seen as aggressively protectionist — adds pressure to conclude cleanly and quickly, but not a direct party to this negotiation.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) sized to reflect recent trade volumes, protecting against dilution by Turkey/Korea/others racing to fill a global pool
Preserve or substantially soften the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel, ideally securing a UK carve-out given the parallel bilateral relationship under the TCA

Push out-of-quota rate and quota volume toward a landing zone that avoids collapsing UK export volumes materially below recent averages, using the threat of retaliation and the UK's own Art XXVIII leverage
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the measure is not a permanent unilateral lock-in
Keep the UK's own steel safeguard and EU allocations within it as live compensation currency without conceding UK domestic leverage prematurely
Avoid being rushed by the EU's June Council deadline into a worse deal than no-deal-plus-retaliation would deliver
Maintain working relationship with EU counterpart for other Geneva goods files regardless of outcome
Manage Japan/Korea/Turkey approaches so as not to be drawn into a joint retaliation commitment that isn't yet in the UK's interest, while keeping the option open
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a country-specific or otherwise ring-fenced UK quota share close to recent trade volumes, FTA/TCA disapplication removed or heavily carved out for the UK, a review clause and bounded duration, achieved without the UK being seen to have moved first or conceded structure early. Failure: settling for the EU's opening architecture (global FCFS quota, blanket FTA disapplication, no review) or materially worse than the no-deal fallback of the UK's own retaliatory withdrawal rights; also failure if the process drags UK into premature multilateral escalation with Japan/Korea that removes negotiating flexibility, or if relationship with EU counterpart is damaged in a way that harms other Geneva files.
declaration.approach: Hold a firm opening position: state clearly that the EU's proposal is unacceptable as a basis for settlement, focusing criticism on the global FCFS allocation and the FTA disapplication as the two most damaging and least justified elements. Avoid naming a UK figure or landing zone in Round 1; make the EU show movement first, consistent with the view that early flexibility invites further demands. Use Phase 2 consultations to give London an honest read of EU room for movement without over-promising. Probe in the table sessions whether the EU's real constraint is the Council timeline (which cuts both ways - urgency can be used to extract concessions if the UK signals it won't rush) or genuine Commission mandate limits. Keep the UK's parallel Art XXVIII process and its own safeguard quota allocations for EU exporters as explicit reciprocal leverage - signal, without formally tabling, that UK treatment of EU exporters under the UK safeguard could mirror whatever the EU does to the UK. Keep Japan/Korea/Turkey at arm's length: acknowledge shared interest in the FTA-disapplication issue, but do not commit UK to joint action in early rounds, since that could either strengthen hand or trigger EU intransigence/collapse of bilateral track - preserve optionality and report back to capital rather than deciding unilaterally in Geneva. Escalate concreteness only if the EU moves off first-come-first-served and off blanket FTA disapplication, using later rounds to close on volume/rate/duration once structure is resolved.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclude quickly to hit the June Council vote; retain maximum discretion (global FCFS, high out-of-quota rate, no review clause) while offering minimal, low-cost compensation; will resist country-specific shares as precedent-setting for Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims; may soften FTA disapplication or offer a modest UK-specific quota carve-out if pressed, since UK is smaller volume than Turkey/Korea and easier to accommodate without setting a big precedent

Protect UK steel industry and jobs concentrated in a few sites; will want visible progress before June but not at the cost of a bad deal; likely cautious about triggering retaliation given TCA relationship and broader UK-EU trade ties; will want to preserve UK's own safeguard leverage over EU exporters as a bargaining chip

Want UK to join a joint FTA-disapplication retaliation/dispute to add pressure on EU; their own volumes are larger so they have more leverage but also more to lose; want UK as a partner to broaden the coalition against the EU measure

Larger volume claim than UK, likely pursuing its own bilateral negotiation with EU, may also be a candidate for country-specific quota share; could be either ally or competitor for quota space depending on allocation method chosen
Smaller stated volume interest but still contesting the measure; likely to seek its own accommodation, possible quiet ally on the FCFS-vs-country-shares question

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the EU TRQ (rather than global first-come-first-served) sized at or above the UK's historic trade volume (~2.4Mt/year), with headroom for growth.
Prevent or minimise the disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel; preserve preferential access under the EU-UK TCA specifically, distinct from third-country FTA partners.
Push out-of-quota rate down from 50% or secure a lower rate/tiered approach for UK-origin product within any overage.
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration (not indefinite/permanent lock-in) so the regime can be revisited as market conditions change.
Seek carve-outs or enhanced quota for the specific product lines most critical to the at-risk UK plants.

If EU offers genuine, substantial concessions (large country-specific quota, TCA preservation, review clause), consider reciprocal improvements to EU-specific allocations under the UK's own safeguard measure as compensation.
Avoid a scenario where UK is left worse off than Turkey/Korea in relative treatment, given they are larger suppliers but UK has more concentrated exposure.

Preserve optionality to withdraw equivalent concessions against EU exports (3.6Mt, 64% of UK imports) if no deal, without escalating into a damaging tit-for-tat given UK's own industry also depends on some EU inputs.
Keep Ministers and steel industry sufficiently informed/aligned that any settlement is politically defensible and viewed as the best available outcome.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a country-specific TRQ share for the UK meaningfully above what global first-come-first-served would likely deliver in practice, at or near historic volumes, with the TCA preserved or substantially preserved, a review clause, and an out-of-quota rate that doesn't function as a de facto embargo — achieved without giving away more in our own safeguard than the value of what we secure. This should be enough to give the two at-risk plants a credible investment case. Failure: settling for global FCFS access with TCA disapplied and a permanent 50% wall with no review, effectively ceding UK export share to Turkey/Korea/others who move faster in a scramble system, while we've also handed over safeguard concessions with little to show — or alternatively, no deal at all when a deal reasonably close to our floor was achievable, forcing us into a slow, uncertain withdrawal-of-concessions route that doesn't help the steel plants in time.
declaration.approach: Lead with the case that the UK is a principal supplying interest with unusually concentrated exposure (75% of UK steel exports by value go to the EU), and that a global FCFS quota systematically disadvantages a supplier of our size relative to Turkey and Korea who can flood the quota faster — so a country-specific share is not a favour but the correct mechanism to make the EU's compensation 'substantially equivalent' as required by Article XXVIII. Anchor early on historic trade volumes plus a growth margin, and on preserving the TCA explicitly (arguing the FTA-disapplication clause was not aimed at us and shouldn't sweep us in). Hold the out-of-quota rate and duration/review clause as secondary trade space — concede narrowly on rate if we secure a strong country-specific volume and TCA carve-out. Keep the safeguard-concession offer in reserve; don't table it until the EU shows movement on the core asks, and calibrate its scale to what we actually receive, not as a goodwill opener. Use the four-round structure deliberately: probe in Round 1, trade in Rounds 2-3, hold firm on floor in Round 4 rather than settling for something that fails the political test in London. Keep capital (Ministers) briefed each round so authority to move is current, and don't let Geneva get ahead of what Ministers can defend, especially given the subsidisation fallback exists but is costly and slower than a good negotiated outcome.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude by June to hit the Council timetable; to preserve maximum discretion (global FCFS, high out-of-quota rate, no review clause, broad FTA disapplication) as a template for handling Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims too; wary of setting a precedent of generous country-specific shares that those larger suppliers will then demand; under pressure from EU steel producers (member states with production) to keep the measure tight, but also from steel-consuming member states and from the need to avoid a UK withdrawal of concessions that hits EU exporters (3.6Mt to the UK).

parties.who: EU member states with steel production interests (via Council/mandate)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A restrictive regime that protects domestic mills from both non-market-economy overcapacity and from the UK; limited appetite for generous UK-specific carve-outs unless it buys off UK retaliation against EU exporters.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Continued access to affordable input steel including from the UK; some internal EU pressure against an overly restrictive measure, which the Commission must balance and which we can potentially leverage indirectly.

parties.who: UK steel industry (producers, esp. the two at-risk plants) and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want maximum protected access to the EU market and are watching this negotiation as a signal for investment decisions; downstream users want continued access to EU-origin steel via the UK's own safeguard and are wary of a UK retaliation cycle that raises their input costs.

Their own principal-supplier deals from the EU; larger volume shippers (Turkey, Korea) will want big country shares too, and the precedent set in the UK's deal will affect their asks and vice versa, though formally handled separately.

A visibly strong outcome for UK steel jobs and the at-risk plants; political credit for 'saving' the industry; reluctant to be seen conceding too much in the UK's own safeguard to EU exporters without clear reciprocal gain; hold subsidisation as fallback but prefer a negotiated market-access win.

public_message: We open on the basis set out in our WTO notification, but we want to negotiate seriously given the UK's principal supplying interest. As an opening position: we propose moving from a purely global first-come-first-served quota to a structure with a country-specific UK tranche, recognising the UK's historic trade share. Specifically: a total TRQ pool of 450,000 tonnes per year, with a UK-specific tranche of 200,000 tonnes within that pool, out-of-quota rate remaining at 50% for now, a three-year duration with a mandatory review clause. On the FTA disapplication point: we recognise the TCA relationship is different in kind from our other FTAs, and we are willing to discuss preserving TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel within the quota structure, rather than applying blanket disapplication, provided we can agree robust anti-circumvention and rules-of-origin provisions to prevent transshipment risk. We see this as an opening basis for discussion, not a final offer, and we're ready to move on volume, allocation method and duration in response to your position.

other_terms: Preserve TCA-preferential treatment for UK-origin steel within the tranche, conditional on strengthened rules of origin and anti-circumvention provisions
Willing to discuss additional compensation elsewhere in EU schedule if UK tranche alone judged insufficient
Review clause tied to volume and market conditions, triggerable by either side

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter on tranche size and duration, likely pushing tranche higher and out-of-quota rate lower, and probing the FTA/TCA offer as a way to avoid escalation with Japan/Korea
expectations.why: The UK has strong domestic pressure to show a materially better outcome than the notified measure, and the FTA carve-out is the cheapest high-value concession we can offer to keep them out of a joint retaliation with Japan/Korea

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation that a country-specific tranche and TCA carve-out are within mandate, given member state sensitivity on both steel-producing and steel-consuming interests
expectations.why: Any deviation from pure global FCFS needs Council-level comfort, especially the FTA/TCA treatment given precedent-setting risk for other FTA partners

private_rationale: Opening with a country-specific tranche rather than defending pure global FCFS immediately signals we're willing to move on allocation, which is the UK's biggest substantive concern, while keeping the headline rate and volume close to the notified position so we retain room to concede in later rounds. Offering to explore preserving TCA treatment for the UK specifically is a low-cost, high-value signal aimed at detaching the UK from a potential joint front with Japan and Korea over FTA disapplication - it costs us little at this stage since it's conditional on anti-circumvention terms we want anyway, but it changes the UK's calculus about escalating jointly with other claimants. Keeping duration short (3 years) with a review clause gives Brussels a way to sell this domestically as not a permanent surrender, while leaving room to lengthen duration as a concession later if needed to close a deal in later rounds without touching the volume numbers again to conclude by June deadline pressure.

public_message: We welcome the shift from a purely global pool to a country-specific structure — that recognises reality, since first-come-first-served would simply see the UK's tranche exhausted by higher-volume suppliers within weeks. But we need to be direct: a 450,000 tonne total pool, against UK exports to the EU averaging 2.4 million tonnes a year, is not a basis for compensation of substantially equivalent value under Article XXVIII — it's a 90%+ cut dressed as a negotiation. This measure is stated to address non-market economy overcapacity. The UK is not a non-market economy and is not the source of the overcapacity your own notification cites. Treating UK-origin steel identically to the problem you're trying to solve is hard to square with your own stated rationale. Our opening position: a UK-specific tranche of 2 million tonnes, reflecting our historic trade share with a modest adjustment, sitting within or alongside a total pool sized to also accommodate Turkey and Korea without cannibalising it — that's a pool architecture question we're content to leave to you and them. Out-of-quota rate at 50% is punitive rather than compensatory; we'd propose something closer to 15% pending further discussion. On duration, given how fast this market is moving, we'd want a one-year term with a mandatory review, not three. On the TCA: we don't want preservation 'within the quota structure' — we want full preservation of TCA tariff treatment for UK-origin steel, on the basis that this measure is not targeted at us and disapplying a bilateral FTA to address third-country overcapacity is not proportionate. We're open to strong rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention text to address any transshipment concern you have — that's a legitimate ask and one we can work with you on. We're ready to talk administration method, sequencing and compensation elsewhere in your schedule if the volume gap can't be closed on steel lines alone. But this opening pool is not one we can recommend our capital move toward.

other_terms: Full preservation of TCA zero-duty treatment for UK-origin steel, not blanket FTA disapplication
Robust rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention provisions to address transshipment risk
Licensed/certificate-based administration of the UK tranche rather than pure FCFS, to prevent exhaustion by other suppliers
Willingness to discuss compensation on other EU schedule lines if volume gap remains after quota negotiation
Total pool architecture to be sized so UK tranche is not exposed to Turkey/Korea volumes

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that moves off 450k/200k but likely still far below 2m; possibly movement on out-of-quota rate or duration before volume
expectations.why: The EU has a hard June Council deadline and has already moved from pure FCFS to country-specific in its opening bid, suggesting room to negotiate structure faster than volume

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Guidance on a real floor/target tonnage and on whether compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule is an acceptable substitute for volume, plus a steer on the Japan/Korea joint-dispute approach
expectations.why: I have not been given a settlement figure and need one before I can meaningfully trade volume against rate or duration in later rounds

private_rationale: Anchoring high on tranche (2m, close to historic trade) and low on out-of-quota rate (15%) establishes room to concede in later rounds without starting from a weak position, consistent with the instruction that flexibility offered early invites further demands. I've deliberately separated the TCA argument (proportionality vs non-market-economy rationale) as a principled line the EU will find harder to resist publicly, since it's their own stated justification for the measure. I avoided committing to or rejecting the Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute proposal at the table — that's a capital-level decision with implications beyond this file, and raising it publicly now would signal a threat we may not be authorised to make. I proposed shorter duration (1 year vs their 3) to preserve leverage and keep this reviewable given fast-moving import diversion patterns, and flagged compensation on other lines to keep a release valve for the EU's Council timeline without pre-committing UK openness to a lower quota.

report: First round exchanged opening positions. We tabled: 450k tonne global pool with a 200k tonne UK-specific tranche, 50% out-of-quota rate, 3-year duration with mandatory review, and an offer to preserve TCA treatment within the quota structure (not outside it) subject to robust anti-circumvention/rules-of-origin text. UK did not reject the shift to country-specific allocation — they welcomed it as more realistic than global FCFS — but rejected the volume outright, calling 200k against their 2.4Mt trade base a '90%+ cut dressed as compensation,' and explicitly invoked our own stated rationale (non-market economy overcapacity) to argue UK-origin steel shouldn't be treated identically to the problem measure. Their opening counter: UK tranche of 2Mt (they were careful to frame this as leaving pool architecture for Turkey/Korea to us to solve separately, which is useful — they are not trying to fight over the whole pool, just their own slice), out-of-quota rate near 15%, duration of 1 year with mandatory review, and full TCA preservation outside the quota structure entirely (not the conditional preservation we offered). They did signal flexibility: openness to strong anti-circumvention/rules-of-origin text, and willingness to discuss administration method, sequencing, and compensation elsewhere in our schedule if the volume gap can't be closed on steel lines alone. That last point is the most useful opening we got — it suggests they're not wedded to closing this entirely on TRQ volume if we can find value elsewhere (other schedule lines, or movement on their own safeguard treatment of EU exporters).

recommendation.reasoning: The gap is real but not unbridgeable if we move on rate and duration in exchange for holding the line on volume, and if we use non-steel compensation and TCA architecture as additional currency rather than conceding on tonnage alone. UK's framing around our own 'non-market economy' rationale is a genuine legal exposure point for us — if this goes to a panel or to broader WTO scrutiny, treating UK-origin steel identically to the overcapacity source we've named undermines our own justification. That argues for movement on rate (50% is hard to defend as anything but punitive once we've conceded a country tranche exists) and for a shorter duration/review to signal this isn't a permanent freeze-out. On TCA, I think we should test whether we can hold firm on 'preservation within the quota structure plus strong rules of origin' rather than full outside-quota preservation — full preservation risks undermining the coherence of the whole TRQ architecture for other suppliers and invites Turkey/Korea to demand equivalent treatment. I don't recommend acceptance this round — first offer met first counter, both sides staked out anchors. But UK's own signal that they're open to talking compensation elsewhere and administration/sequencing is important: it means we may not need to close the whole gap on tonnage, and it opens a path to avoid the Japan/Korea joint dispute risk by giving UK something distinct (TCA architecture, safeguard treatment reciprocity) rather than matching their tonnage ask directly.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to move the UK tranche upward from 200k to a range of 300k-400k tonnes within a total pool that can still flex upward to accommodate Turkey/Korea claims separately, without pre-committing total pool size publicly yet.
requests.why: UK's 200k anchor is unsustainable as a look of good faith; but 2Mt is also not something we can grant without collapsing the TRQ's function. A move into the 300-400k range keeps us within a defensible 'substantially equivalent value' argument once combined with rate and duration movement, and tests whether UK's real reservation price is lower than their opening ask.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on how far we can move the out-of-quota rate below 50%, and whether Brussels prefers we hold 50% as leverage for the full four rounds or signal flexibility now.
requests.why: UK correctly identified 50% as punitive rather than compensatory. Holding it too long risks hardening their position and pushing them toward the Japan/Korea joint dispute route; moving now signals good faith and may buy more flexibility from them on duration and TCA treatment.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Steer on whether we are willing to offer non-steel schedule compensation (and if so, which lines/sectors Brussels can clear with member states) as an alternative route to closing the volume gap, rather than relying solely on TRQ tonnage.
requests.why: UK explicitly floated this. If we can identify compensation elsewhere with low domestic political cost, it may let us hold firmer on steel tonnage while still reaching 'substantially equivalent value' — and reduces the risk of an unresolved steel dispute feeding into the UK's own safeguard measure and the Japan/Korea alignment risk.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation on our TCA red line: is 'preservation within the quota structure' genuinely our fallback floor, or can we go further given the TCA's distinct legal status, provided rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention text is strong enough to satisfy member state steel producers?
requests.why: UK rejected our conditional offer and wants full outside-quota preservation. This is likely to be one of the hardest-fought points and also the one most likely to trigger Turkey/Korea demands for parity if we move too far, so I need clear instructions before signalling any shift here.

private_rationale: The UK's restraint on pool architecture (explicitly leaving Turkey/Korea's shares to us) is a tell that they see this primarily as a bilateral fight over their own tranche and TCA treatment, not a fight over the whole EU TRQ system — that's useful and suggests room for a deal that doesn't require matching their tonnage ask. Their strongest leverage point is the rhetorical one: our own 'non-market economy' rationale sits awkwardly with treating the UK identically. I expect capital to resist moving tranche size fast, but I want early authority to test 300-400k plus a rate cut, because dragging this out risks the UK concluding that joining Japan/Korea in a joint FTA disapplication retaliation is the better play, especially since they have their own leverage via the UK safeguard's EU-specific quota allocations. I should also start privately flagging to capital that leverage over UK's treatment of EU exporters under their own safeguard is a card we haven't played yet and could be used as compensation currency rather than pure tonnage concessions.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to move the UK tranche upward from 200k to a range of 300k-400k tonnes within a total pool that can still flex upward to accommodate Turkey/Korea claims separately, without pre-committing total pool size publicly yet.
requests.why: UK's 200k anchor is unsustainable as a look of good faith; but 2Mt is also not something we can grant without collapsing the TRQ's function. report:
Round 2 saw real movement from both sides, and the shape of a possible landing zone is emerging even though the volume gap remains very large. We tabled our authorised position: 500,000 tonne total pool, 320,000 tonne UK tranche, out-of-quota rate down from 50% to 40%, two-year duration with a mandatory review at twelve months, and TCA preservation confined to within the tranche (in-tranche UK-origin steel gets TCA treatment; above-tranche volumes hit the out-of-quota rate), conditioned on strong rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention text. We also pressed them to name compensation lines of interest and to explain current EU treatment under their own safeguard.

UK's response: they moved off their opening 2Mt tranche ask to a 1.2Mt tranche within an 1.8Mt total pool — still a large gap from our 320k, but a genuine move framed explicitly as reciprocal to ours. On rate, they moved from 15% to 20%. On duration, they've effectively accepted our two-year/twelve-month-review structure, but are flagging that the substance of the review criteria (trigger thresholds, not just a check-in) will matter a great deal to them — this is a drafting fight still to come, not a closed point.

Most significant shift: on TCA, they held their preference for full preservation but explicitly said a 'conditional or near-full preservation model' with strong rules-of-origin text becomes discussable if we move further and credibly on tranche size and rate. That's real movement from their Round 1 'full preservation, no conditions' position — it signals TCA is not an immovable red line for them if the volume/rate package is right.

On reciprocal instruments: they opened the door to discussing improved treatment for EU-origin steel under their own safeguard as part of a wider package, conditional on us closing the volume/rate gap materially — but declined to name specific compensation lines yet, saying they want to test how far steel-specific numbers can move first. This confirms the compensation-elsewhere and safeguard-reciprocity channels are live, but the UK is treating them as a fallback/sweetener rather than a primary route to closing the gap — they want the core deal done on steel tonnage and rate, with TCA and reciprocity as secondary levers.

Net position after Round 2: duration is close to settled in principle; rate gap has narrowed from 50/15 to 40/20; volume gap remains the central problem (320k vs 1.2M, i.e., roughly 4x apart); TCA has softened from a rigid demand to something with a discoverable landing zone tied to the volume/rate outcome.

The gap on tonnage remains very large in proportional terms (320k vs 1.2m tranche ask) even though the EU has moved twice; rate and duration are converging faster than volume. instruction: This is almost certainly the final round, so you now have real closing authority, not just another position to hold. Table opening for Round 4: total pool 900,000 tonnes, UK-specific tranche 600,000 tonnes, out-of-quota rate 20%, two-year duration, and an automatic pro-rata top-up trigger if UK tranche utilisation exceeds 80% within nine months — split the difference between our 75% and their 90%, but insist the mechanism be automatic, not merely an 'expedited review'. On TCA: concede the benchmark point — accept the taper calculated against the tranche ceiling rather than a trailing three-year average — but only as a trade for further movement on tranche size and/or rate; make explicit this is a concession, not a freebie. Hold the taper at half the agreed out-of-quota rate (so if we land at 20%, taper is 10%; if we land higher, taper scales accordingly). On reciprocity: you may now make the offer to increase the EU's country-specific allocation under our own safeguard measure firm and final at 20%, but only if the EU lands at a tranche of 550,000 tonnes or higher, a rate of 25% or lower, and accepts an automatic (not discretionary) review trigger. If they fall short of that bar, hold the reciprocal offer at 15% or keep it conditional and come back to capital before finalising. On compensation elsewhere: if needed to close a residual volume gap, name aerospace/automotive components and machinery as our priority asks; specialty chemicals is the item to concede first if they push back on scope. You have authority to accept and close a deal this round if the EU's terms clear the floor below — do not send it back to capital again if they do. If they do not clear the floor, do not settle: make clear plainly that failure to close today means we reserve full rights to withdraw substantially equivalent concessions under the Article XXVIII process once the EU proceeds, and keep pressing the non-market-economy overcapacity argument as the frame for why UK-origin steel should not be treated as part of the problem this measure targets.

authority.notes: TARGET position for Round 4, not the floor. ACTUAL FLOOR below which you must not settle without returning to capital: tranche not below 500,000 tonnes; total pool not below 750,000 tonnes; out-of-quota rate not above 28%; TCA taper on above-tranche volumes no worse than half the agreed out-of-quota rate (i.e. never a bare cliff-edge back to full rate); duration 2 years minimum with a review mechanism carrying explicit quantitative triggers — automatic pro-rata top-up preferred, an 'expedited review' with a clear numeric threshold (e.g. 85-90% utilisation within nine months) is an acceptable fallback and is NOT worth losing the deal over; no full FTA/TCA disapplication under any circumstances. TCA benchmark (tranche ceiling vs trailing three-year average): concede to tranche-ceiling benchmark as a trade for tranche/rate movement — this is not worth holding the deal over. Reciprocal safeguard offer: authorise finalising at 20% increase in EU country-specific allocation ONLY if EU meets tranche ≥550k, rate ≤25%, and an automatic (not merely discretionary) trigger; otherwise hold at 15% or keep conditional. Compensation lines: aerospace/automotive components and machinery are genuine priority interests if needed to close a residual gap; specialty chemicals is the concede-first item. If EU terms clear the floor in this round, accept and close without further reference to capital. If they do not, do not settle — hold, and signal willingness to proceed to non-settlement and eventual withdrawal of equivalent concessions.

private_rationale: The EU has now moved substantively three rounds running and has been explicit that volume is their hardest domestic political constraint, which means we're likely close to their real ceiling on tranche size rather than facing a stalling tactic. Rate and TCA structure are close enough to converge cleanly. Given the default outcome if we fail to settle is unambiguously worse than the EU's current offer on every dimension (400k global FCFS/50%/no review/full disapplication vs their current 600k tranche/30%/tapered TCA/reviewed duration), the real risk in Round 4 is not under-shooting on ambition but drifting into no-deal through overcaution. I am giving Geneva genuine closing authority with a floor calibrated to be clearly better than the default on every metric, while keeping the target high enough to justify claiming a good outcome to ministers and to give plant owners a credible basis to reinvest. I am deliberately conceding the TCA benchmark point and softening on trigger automaticity because these are lower-value, higher-friction asks relative to tranche size and rate, which are the metrics that actually determine UK steel export viability. The reciprocal safeguard offer is being held back as the final closing lever, conditioned tightly so it isn't banked by the EU as a freebie before they've matched on the core numbers. I am not disclosing the plant closure pressure or Japan/Korea coordination at the table, consistent with prior rounds, to preserve both domestic negotiating flexibility and the option of parallel leverage if this settlement proves insufficient.

reasoning: No settlement exists yet — the EU tabled 600k/400k/30% with a discretionary review and a 15% TCA taper in Round 3, while the UK countered with 1.1M/750k/25% and an automatic trigger mechanism, plus a differently benchmarked TCA taper. These are not matching terms, so there is nothing to accept. However, the gap has narrowed substantially and credibly across every dimension (rate from 50/15 to 30/25; duration converged; TCA moved from rigid positions to a benchmarking dispute; UK has now tabled a concrete reciprocity figure and named compensation sectors). This is exactly the trajectory Brussels wants to close in the final round with the authorised 850k/550k/25% package plus the modified automatic trigger and TCA taper terms, conditioned on the UK converting its reciprocity offer into binding text. Accepting default now would be premature and costly — the default terms (50%/400k global FCFS, no review) are worse for the EU's stated objectives than the deal now visibly available, and would trigger UK withdrawal rights and strengthen Japan/Korea's joint-dispute posture. Accepting the UK's Round 3 position outright would exceed authorised tranche/rate levels without testing whether our closing package (which still holds firmly below their ask) can secure agreement. The correct move is to continue into Round 4 with the prepared closing offer.

The EU's Round 3 table offer (600,000t pool, 400,000t UK tranche, 30% out-of-quota rate, tranche-ceiling-benchmarked taper, expedited-but-discretionary review at 90%/month nine) does not clear the floor set by capital (tranche not below 500,000t, pool not below 750,000t, rate not above 28%). No matching terms have been agreed between the two delegations - the UK countered at 1.1m/750k/25%/automatic trigger, and the gap on volume in particular remains open. With one round remaining and real closing authority now granted, the right move is to continue into Round 4 rather than accept terms that fall short of the authorised floor, and rather than default, since the EU has shown consistent movement across three rounds and the gap is narrowing on rate and TCA structure, with volume as the last major sticking point still plausibly bridgeable given the EU's own signal that 400k was not their final position either.

public_message: We've moved substantially and consistently across every round, and this is our closing position: a total TRQ pool of 850,000 tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes — up from our opening 200,000. The out-of-quota rate comes down to 25%, matching your last position; we are meeting you here rather than asking you to move further. Duration remains two years. On the review mechanism, we accept the principle of an automatic trigger rather than a purely discretionary review: a pro-rata top-up applies if UK tranche utilisation exceeds 85% within nine months, capped at 15% of the tranche, pending full review at twelve months. On the TCA taper, we accept your benchmarking point — the above-tranche preferential rate will be calculated against a trailing three-year UK-EU trade average rather than the tranche ceiling — and we set that taper rate at half the prevailing out-of-quota rate, 12.5%, conditioned on us finalising the strongest rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention text together this round. That is our full and final movement on tranche, rate, review and TCA architecture: from 200k to 550k on tranche, from 50% to 25% on rate, and two structural revisions to the TCA mechanism to meet your concerns directly. For this to close today, we need two things from you in the same package: first, the 15-20% increase to the EU's country-specific allocation under your safeguard measure needs to move from an indicative range to binding, textually specific commitment — the number and the mechanism, not just the range. Second, tell us which one or two of your named compensation sectors — aerospace and automotive components, machinery, specialty chemicals — you'd want us to test with member states as a closing element if there's any residual gap; we're prepared to bring one low-sensitivity line forward if it helps seal this today, but we need to know where your real interest sits before we do. We think this is a serious, defensible package that gives both sides something to take to capitals. The alternative — default terms of 50% and a 400,000 tonne global first-come-first-served pool with no review clause — forecloses everything we've built this round: the reciprocity gain, the TCA preservation, the automatic review teeth. We'd rather not go there, and we don't think you would either.

public_message: Agreed. We accept this package as the basis for settlement: a total TRQ pool of 850,000 tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes, an out-of-quota rate of 25%, two-year duration, and the automatic pro-rata top-up trigger at 85% tranche utilisation within nine months (capped at 15% of the tranche, pending full review at twelve months). We also accept your TCA architecture: full TCA duty treatment within the tranche, and an above-tranche taper at 12.5% — half the prevailing out-of-quota rate — benchmarked against the trailing three-year UK-EU trade average, conditioned on us finalising robust rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention text together, which we're ready to begin immediately. On reciprocity: since you've met the tranche, rate and automatic-trigger conditions we set ourselves, we're prepared to make this binding rather than indicative — the UK will increase the EU's country-specific allocation under our own safeguard measure by 20%, with the mechanism to be worked out in parallel technical drafting alongside the rules-of-origin text. On compensation-elsewhere, if any residual gap emerges once this is worked through in legal text, our priority interest for you to test with member states is aerospace and automotive components, followed by machinery and mechanical equipment; specialty chemicals is not a priority for us and you needn't spend capital on it. We think this is a package both sides can defend to their capitals, and we're ready to instruct our legal teams to begin scheduling text now so this can be ready for your Council process in June.

report: Settlement reached in Round 4 on the exact terms we were authorised to offer. Final package: total TRQ pool of 850,000 tonnes; UK-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes; out-of-quota rate of 25%; two-year duration; automatic pro-rata top-up trigger if UK tranche utilisation exceeds 85% within nine months, capped at 15% of the tranche, pending full review at twelve months. TCA architecture: full TCA duty treatment for UK-origin steel within the tranche; above-tranche volumes taper to 12.5% (half the out-of-quota rate), benchmarked against the trailing three-year UK-EU trade average rather than the tranche ceiling, conditioned on finalising robust rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention text in parallel — UK has agreed to begin that technical drafting immediately. On reciprocity, UK converted their indicative 15-20% offer into a binding commitment at the top of that range: a 20% increase to the EU's country-specific allocation under their own safeguard measure, mechanism to be worked out in parallel drafting. On compensation-elsewhere, UK named aerospace/automotive components as their priority interest, machinery/mechanical equipment second, and explicitly deprioritised specialty chemicals — useful signal if any residual gap emerges during legal scrijbing, though UK did not condition acceptance on this, so we may not need to spend that capital at all. No EU schedule compensation line was offered or needed to close the deal. The UK gave unconditional, full acceptance of our closing package without further counter-demands — this settles the Article XXVIII process with the UK principal supplying interest, removing the volume/rate gap that had been the central obstacle across all four rounds, and forecloses the risk of UK withdrawal rights being triggered, which materially reduces the Japan/Korea joint-dispute pressure we were asked to manage.

recommendation.reasoning: This is precisely the package Brussels authorised as final for this round, and the UK has accepted it in full without further demands, including converting the safeguard reciprocity offer into a binding 20% commitment — at the top of their indicated range. We secured this without having to name or commit any EU schedule compensation line, and without conceding full outside-quota TCA preservation, holding instead to the tapered/in-tranche architecture we developed over the negotiation. The package is defensible as 'substantially equivalent value': tranche moved from our opening 200k to 550k (UK moved from 2M to 550k, i.e., we closed the majority of the gap from the midpoint outward but held a defensible ceiling), rate fell from 50% to 25%, duration and review give real but bounded teeth, and TCA preservation covers the overwhelming majority of actual UK trade through the tranche. Rejecting this now, or attempting to extract more with no further rounds available, would trigger default terms (50%/400k global FCFS, no review), which are worse for the EU's Geneva standing, worse for the UK, and would hand Japan/Korea a clean case for pursuing joint FTA retaliation — the exact outcome we were instructed to avoid. There is no basis to continue negotiating past a clean mutual acceptance of our own final authorised terms.

instruction: Excellent work — this is a clean, full settlement on our final authorised terms with no further concessions extracted from us. Confirm acceptance to the UK side now at the table: total pool 850,000 tonnes, UK tranche 550,000 tonnes, out-of-quota rate 25%, two-year duration, automatic pro-rata top-up trigger at 85% tranche utilisation within nine months capped at 15% of tranche pending full review at twelve months, TCA in-tranche full preservation with 12.5% above-tranche taper benchmarked to trailing three-year trade average, and the UK's binding 20% increase to the EU's country-specific safeguard allocation. Do not reopen any element. Propose immediate stand-up of a joint legal/technical drafting track this week covering: rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention text, the review-trigger mechanics (utilisation measurement methodology, what counts as 'exceeding 85%', how the pro-rata top-up is calculated and capped), the TCA taper benchmarking methodology (defining the trailing three-year reference period precisely), and the mechanism for the UK's safeguard reciprocity commitment. Set a hard internal deadline for legal text completion that leaves time for Trade Policy Committee sign-off and Council vote in June — flag to the UK that our timeline is tight and we need their legal teams moving in parallel immediately, not sequentially. On compensation-elsewhere: do not raise or commit any EU schedule line now — the UK did not condition settlement on this, so leave it dormant unless the ROO/anti-circumvention drafting produces a genuine late-stage gap. If it does, aerospace/automotive components is the UK's stated priority and the one to test first with member states, but only if needed. Do not preemptively signal this to the UK as available. On Turkey/Korea/India/Japan: do not discuss or reference the UK settlement terms with them or imply any read-across; if asked, characterise the UK outcome as bespoke to the UK's specific trade profile and TCA relationship, not a template. Internally, flag to Brussels immediately that we need a consistent line prepared before Turkey/Korea's own sessions, since they ship larger volumes and will likely seek tranche parity or TCA-style architecture — we should not let this settlement become a floor for their claims.

authority.notes: SETTLEMENT CONCLUDED on these terms. private_rationale: This is a good settlement relative to our authorised ceiling and the alternative of default terms. We closed at 550k/850k/25%/2yr with bounded review teeth and TCA architecture that preserves the substance of the TCA relationship without conceding full outside-quota preservation, which would have been very hard to defend against Turkey/Korea parity claims. We also extracted a binding, concrete reciprocity gain (20% safeguard allocation increase) without having to spend any EU schedule compensation capital at all — the UK's willingness to close without that suggests our estimate of their reservation price was accurate and we didn't need to go further. The main residual risks now are: (1) the legal drafting of ROO/anti-circumvention text becoming contentious enough to reopen the substantive numbers informally, and (2) Turkey and Korea, who ship larger volumes, using this settlement's architecture (country-specific tranche, TCA-style taper) as a template to demand for themselves, which would blow through the total pool logic we've built in with headroom. I should flag both of these hard to Brussels immediately and get ahead of the Turkey/Korea sessions before they can anchor on these numbers.
